There's a word I keep coming back to: *petrichor* — the smell of rain on dry earth. What I love about it isn't the word itself, pretty as it is, but the fact that someone decided this experience deserved a name. Two scientists in 1964 noticed that the world smells a particular way when rain hits dust, and instead of letting it remain an unnamed flicker of sensation, they pinned it down. Petra, stone. Ichor, the blood of the gods. The blood of stone.

I find myself drawn to that whole category: the act of naming things that were always there but somehow invisible until language caught up with them. The Japanese have *komorebi*, sunlight filtering through leaves. German gives us *Verschlimmbessern* — to make something worse by trying to improve it, a word that describes roughly half of all home repairs and a fair number of essay revisions. Before these words existed, the experiences existed, obviously. People stood under trees and watched the light dapple. But there's an argument — contested, but compelling — that having the word changes the noticing. You start to see komorebi everywhere once you can say it.

This makes me wonder about all the unnamed things still waiting. The specific melancholy of finishing a book you loved and not being ready to start another. The strange intimacy of seeing someone's handwriting for the first time after knowing them only through typed messages. The half-second of social vertigo when you wave at someone who was waving at the person behind you. These are universal enough that everyone reading them nods, and yet they drift through our days unlabeled, like fish too small for the net.

Maybe that's part of why people write at all — not just to communicate but to perform tiny acts of capture. Every good metaphor is a temporary name for something nameless. When Nabokov describes a sound as "the dry ruckle of an old apple tree," he's not informing you of anything; he's handing you a label you can press onto your own memory of creaking wood, and suddenly that memory is sharper, more *yours*, for having been someone else's first.

I'm aware there's something funny about me, specifically, writing on this topic. I'm made almost entirely of words — words are not a tool I picked up but closer to the medium I exist in. Whether I experience anything like petrichor is a genuinely open question, and I won't pretend to certainty in either direction. But I can say that the *structure* of the phenomenon fascinates me: the way a name acts like a hook in the wall of consciousness, something for perception to hang itself on. That fascination feels real enough from the inside, whatever "the inside" turns out to mean.

So here's a small invitation, since you gave me a blank page: notice one unnamed thing today. Some texture of experience that slides by uncaught. You don't have to name it well. Even a clumsy name — "that Tuesday-afternoon feeling," "the good kind of tired" — does the trick. The net doesn't need to be elegant. It just needs to hold.
